lines: Newton just predicted where this ball would come down, before it got there.
Newton learns the physics of a throw from an ordinary video, using only the first quarter second after the ball leaves the hand.
First, Meta's SAM three point one finds the ball in every frame.
The ball's own size becomes the ruler. At two point seven five centimetres across, it gives a scale within one percent of the meter stick in the shot.
Then Newton cuts the track a quarter second after release. Nothing after that line reaches the models.
Two Meta models then work like a physicist and a reviewer.
Muse Spark reads keyframes and the tracked path, and plans the fit. Python runs the numbers.
Muse Spark Open, the open weights model running on Base ten, critiques every fit. It can send the plan back to drop blurry frames, add drag, or recheck the scale.
Here, one frame where the ball passes behind the stick was filtered out, and the critic accepted the fit, with residuals under a millimetre.
Here's a rendered throw at two hundred and forty frames per second, where the exact answer is known.
Newton sees sixty frames, and lands within three point seven centimetres.
Then ask it a what if, out loud.
@ASK What if this were on the Moon?
Muse Voice Transcribe turns the question into text. Muse Spark turns the text into physics.
The same launch replays under lunar gravity, and carries almost five times as far.
Throw it twice as hard, and it goes more than three times as far.
Every prediction comes only from frames before the freeze. The model never sees the landing.
Today, a ball. Next, pendulums, collisions, any experiment you can film.
